## Depth: Communicating Across Levels
Designing with data aims to reduce reliance on 'gut' decision-making, which consequently breaks hierarchical structures. A company-wide data literacy culture, built on addressing well-formulated, carefully investigated questions, invites discussion, challenge, and the acceptance of being wrong. This data is best collected using diverse methods—not just A/B testing, but also ethnographic field research, field deployments of prototypes, surveys, lab studies, and usability research. Grounded user data is a less risky prospect than relying on hunches from individual executives.

A 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield, 'Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO,' illustrates the underlying principle: data is an effective way to resolve conflicts in decision making without relying on rank, hierarchy, or company politics.

John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, notes that data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation within the company.

Patty McCord, former Netflix Chief Talent Officer, explains that having a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for your customers allows more people to have a voice in product development. The data-driven approach succeeded at Netflix because the practice was well established and universally accepted. It started at the top with CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt believing in its value, but was embraced by everyone from management to individual contributors.

Patty states that at Netflix, even the CEO doesn't get to do whatever he wants. Executives can get caught up in thinking they know the answer, but embracing A/B testing mitigates top-down problem-solving because everyone learns from experimentation. For example, Reed Hastings would submit his product ideas to the same rigor of A/B testing as the product team. On rare occasions, he might dictate an implementation on 'his test cell' (the experimental group he was backing), which would be tested against cells proposed by the product team. If it didn't win, it didn't launch. This accountability reinforced subjecting ideas to grounded review and viewing 'failure' as a positive outcome.

When shifting to a data-aware framework, examine existing decision-making processes. If decisions were concentrated in one or two individuals, ensure they understand the value of incorporating user data, as it may diminish the weight of any single opinion, including your own. It is critical to check if you are comfortable with how incorporating data will change the weight of your own opinion within the design and product development process.

## Overview of Statistical Approach
This appendix details the statistical methods used to analyze survey data from over 2,000 organizations to identify capabilities driving software delivery and organizational performance. The research used a cross-sectional survey design and Partial Least Squares (PLS) path modeling to test a theoretical model linking technical, process, cultural, and leadership capabilities to outcomes. PLS was chosen because it is suitable for exploratory research, complex models, and prediction-oriented analysis, and it makes fewer distributional assumptions than covariance-based structural equation modeling (SEM).

## Survey Design and Data Collection
Data came from annual State of DevOps surveys (2014-2017), using a 7-point Likert scale. To mitigate common method bias, the design followed Dillman's tailored design method, used different scale endpoints, separated predictor and outcome variables, and employed a marker variable technique (Lindell & Whitney, 2001). The marker variable was a theoretically unrelated construct used to adjust correlations for common method variance.

## Measurement Model Validation
The measurement model was validated first. Internal consistency reliability was confirmed via composite reliability scores (>0.7), which is preferred over Cronbach's alpha for PLS. Convergent validity was established with indicator loadings >0.7 and average variance extracted (AVE) >0.5. Discriminant validity was confirmed using the Fornell-Larcker criterion (square root of AVE greater than correlations with other constructs). This ensures constructs are distinct.

## Structural Model and Hypothesis Testing
PLS path modeling tested relationships between capabilities and two outcomes: software delivery performance (a latent construct measured by deployment frequency, lead time, mean time to restore, and change fail rate) and organizational performance (profitability, productivity, market share). Bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples tested significance. Software delivery performance strongly predicted organizational performance (path coefficient = 0.42, p < 0.001). The analysis identified 24 key capabilities driving software delivery performance. The model's predictive relevance was assessed using Stone-Geisser's Q² (cross-validated redundancy), with values >0 indicating predictive relevance.

## Controls and Robustness Checks
Control variables for organization size and industry were included; they did not change the significance of main relationships. Robustness checks included testing alternative model specifications (e.g., direct effects from capabilities to organizational performance), examining mediation effects (confirming software delivery performance fully mediated the relationship for most capabilities), and cross-validation by splitting data by year to ensure consistency across cohorts. The stability of path coefficients and R² values across years was confirmed.

## Key Statistical Findings
The relationship between software delivery performance and organizational performance is statistically significant and positive, with a substantial effect size. The identified capabilities explain a significant portion of the variance in software delivery performance (R² values), supporting the model's explanatory power. The research demonstrates that the link between technical capabilities and organizational outcomes is not merely correlational but is mediated by measurable software delivery performance.

## Overview of Statistical Approach
This appendix details the statistical methods used to analyze survey data from over 2,000 organizations to identify capabilities that drive software delivery performance and organizational outcomes. The research employed a cross-sectional survey design and used Partial Least Squares (PLS) path modeling for analysis. The goal was to test a theoretical model linking technical, process, cultural, and leadership capabilities to performance outcomes while rigorously validating the measurement instruments.

## Survey Design and Data Collection
The data came from the annual State of DevOps surveys conducted from 2014 to 2017, yielding responses from over 2,000 organizations each year. The survey used a 7-point Likert scale for most items. To mitigate common method bias, the survey design followed Dillman's tailored design method, used different scale endpoints, and separated predictor and outcome variables. A marker variable technique (Lindell & Whitney, 2001) was also employed to test for common method variance.

## Measurement Model Validation
Before testing the structural model, the researchers validated the measurement model to ensure constructs were measured reliably and validly. They assessed internal consistency reliability using composite reliability scores, with all constructs exceeding the recommended threshold of 0.7. Convergent validity was established by examining indicator reliability (all loadings > 0.7) and average variance extracted (AVE > 0.5 for all constructs). Discriminant validity was confirmed using the Fornell-Larcker criterion, where the square root of each construct's AVE was greater than its correlations with other constructs.

## Structural Model and Hypothesis Testing
The core analysis used Partial Least Squares (PLS) path modeling, chosen for its ability to handle complex models with many constructs and its suitability for prediction-oriented research. The model included four categories of capabilities: technical, process, cultural, and leadership. The analysis tested the relationships between these capabilities and two key outcomes: software delivery performance (a latent construct measured by deployment frequency, lead time, mean time to restore, and change fail rate) and organizational performance (profitability, productivity, and market share).

Bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples was used to test the statistical significance of the path coefficients. The results showed that software delivery performance strongly and positively predicts organizational performance (path coefficient = 0.42, p < 0.001). The analysis also identified 24 key capabilities that drive software delivery performance, which are detailed in Appendix A.

## Controls and Robustness Checks
The model included control variables for organization size (number of employees) and industry. These controls did not change the significance of the main relationships. Additional robustness checks involved testing alternative model specifications and examining potential mediation effects. The researchers also conducted a cross-validation by splitting the data by year to ensure the results were consistent across different survey cohorts.

## Key Statistical Findings
The analysis confirmed that the relationship between software delivery performance and organizational performance is statistically significant and positive. The effect size is substantial, indicating that improvements in software delivery directly contribute to better organizational outcomes. The research also demonstrated that the identified capabilities explain a significant portion of the variance in software delivery performance (R² values), supporting the model's explanatory power.

## Coordinating Retirement
British Airways (BA) aimed to retire Concorde with Air France in October 2003. Air France retired in May 2003 instead, reflecting differing attitudes and the impossibility of a joint celebratory retirement post-accident.

## Announcement and Messaging
BA announced the retirement to senior management on April 10, 2003, avoiding the April 9 anniversary of the first flight. Chief Pilot Mike Bannister delivered the news; internal reaction split roughly two-thirds sadness to one-third relief. Bannister became the spokesman, stressing a commercial decision due to factors beyond BA's control, not the 2000 accident. He coined the official line: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons."

## Addressing Challenges
*   **Richard Branson/Virgin Atlantic:** BA's official response was that transfer of ownership, due to original UK government funding, was not BA's decision. A senior Virgin pilot privately confided taking Concorde "would probably send us bust."
*   **Retaining a Single Aircraft:** Keeping one Concorde for displays was unfeasible. As a passenger aircraft, it required a full Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate, unlike display aircraft like the Vulcan bomber on a 'Permit to Fly'. Infrastructure costs were immense—estimated at up to £1 million per week for one aircraft. Airbus, as the Type Certificate holder, was unwilling to support continued operation, partly due to proprietary secret technology in systems like the air-intake computers.

## Shift in Public Sentiment
By summer 2003, public discussion shifted to celebrating Concorde's legacy, highlighting UK achievement and public pride. BA framed the final phase as a celebration of everyone involved, and the public, many of whom felt a personal sense of ownership.

## Coordinating and Announcing the Retirement
British Airways (BA) sought to coordinate Concorde's retirement with Air France, initially aiming for a simultaneous October 2003 end. Air France, however, decided to retire its fleet in May 2003 instead, reflecting differing attitudes and the impossibility of a joint celebratory retirement in post-accident France.

## Internal and Public Announcement
BA planned to announce the retirement to senior management via the 'Forum 150' network on April 9, 2003, but switched to April 10 to avoid the 34th anniversary of Concorde's first flight. As Chief Pilot, Mike Bannister delivered the news. Internal reaction split roughly two-thirds sadness to one-third relief, presaging the public response.

## Managing Public Relations and Key Messages
Bannister became the company spokesman. Core messages stressed the retirement was a commercial decision due to factors beyond BA's control, not the 2000 accident, and that customers would be looked after via upgraded 747 services. Bannister coined the official line: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons."

## Addressing Specific Challenges
*   **Richard Branson/Virgin Atlantic:** BA anticipated Branson's offer to operate Concorde. The official response was that transfer of ownership, due to original UK government funding, was not BA's decision. A senior Virgin pilot privately confided taking Concorde "would probably send us bust."
*   **Retaining a Single Aircraft:** Keeping one Concorde for displays was deemed unfeasible. As a passenger aircraft, it required a full Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate, unlike display aircraft like the Vulcan bomber on a 'Permit to Fly'. Associated infrastructure costs were immense—estimated at up to £1 million per week for one aircraft. Airbus, as the manufacturer and Type Certificate holder, was focused on new projects like the A380 and was unwilling to support continued operation, partly due to proprietary secret technology in systems like the air-intake computers.

## Shift in Public Sentiment
Public discussion shifted from retirement motives to celebrating Concorde's legacy by summer 2003. The narrative highlighted UK achievement, successful operation, and public pride. BA framed the final phase as a celebration of everyone involved with the aircraft and the public, many of whom felt a personal sense of ownership.
